narrative: A young man from a wealthy Aleppo family - his father a businessman and university professor, his mother a teacher - studied civil engineering at university, where he met his wife. They married in 2013 before he finished his studies, and their first son was born in 2014. When the war reached Aleppo in 2015 it became dangerous even to get food; there was no electricity, water or internet. He and his wife fled through the night, with snipers everywhere, to his parents in Turkey. His father tried to arrange a regular visa through the German embassy in Ankara, without success, then returned to Syria to settle affairs and was never heard from again; after six months the family assumed he was dead. His mother gave him money to escape, and his wife, who wanted to return to her own parents in Syria, stayed behind in Turkey with the plan that she would join him later with their son. He went to Izmir with a group of eight, but it took a week to find a smuggler they could trust, who would take them for $1,000 a person. When the smuggler learned his wife and young son were still in Turkey, he urged him to bring them immediately, knowing how hard family reunification would be; they arrived by bus the same day, and the next day the three of them took the boat to Greece with the others. As soon as they reached European waters a larger ship picked them up. They were photographed and fed in the camp on the island, but it had been overcrowded for months so they paid to stay outside it; their son injured his foot during those days. After three days they were given documents and taken to Athens on a large ship, where they spent two days in a cheap hotel. Then a bus to Macedonia, and from there they walked to the Serbian border; to this day he does not know why they were not sent back to Greece. In Serbia he collected money sent by his sister's husband. From Serbia they took a bus toward Hungary, but were captured in the forest by Hungarian police, interned and photographed. Their son had a severe fever, and the Red Cross treated his foot infection. An Algerian translator threatened them with a gun to extort fingerprints, but he claimed they were going to Sweden and did not need to give them. They left the camp after 24 hours and, a few kilometers on, caught a cab to Vienna, then a train to Germany. In Duesseldorf they went to the police: 'We are refugees from Syria.' They were treated kindly, taken by ambulance to a children's hospital for their son and then to another hospital for his malnourished wife. They moved through camps in Dortmund - the first chaotic, the second with families and a play corner - and after 20 days were transferred to a small apartment that turned out to be moldy, then to a better one, where two neighbors became like a new family over the following years. He now has three children in elementary school, but his unfinished degree was never recognized, which he says left him a person with a broken back; his studies had been his dream.
